weeks.state:
You are the replenishment planner for one product. Each week you place one order before customers buy. Stock sells at $14 a unit and costs $5; every order also costs a fixed $10. Unsold stock carries over and costs $4 a unit per week. Each unit of demand you can't meet costs $10 in lost goodwill on top of the lost sale. At the end of the plan leftovers are cleared at $0 a unit. Usual weekly demand is about 10 units, lower in a slow spell and much higher in a surge. Notes in your inbox vary in reliability: rumours are often wrong, sales reps are usually right, written customer confirmations rarely wrong.

Week 1 of 4 (4 including this one left in the plan).
Stock on hand now: 0 units.
Inbox:
- (this week) Our rep covering Pinecrest Markets reports that no change to their typical pull.

order.instructions: How many units should the planner order this week to maximise profit over the rest of the plan?

regime.instructions: What is customer demand most likely doing this week?

hypotheses.statement: A JEV-style model is strong from the start, where RL starts near random.
hypotheses.rule: Supported if Kev zero-shot beats every PPO variant's untrained score by >= 20 points of % optimal (mean over horizons); not supported if it doesn't beat them at all.
hypotheses.evidence: Kev zero-shot starts +38.4 points of % optimal vs the best untrained PPO (mean over horizons).

hypotheses.statement: A JEV-style model improves more slowly with training; RL catches up or overtakes.
hypotheses.rule: Supported if Kev+RL gains fewer points per 10x data than the best PPO variant in most horizons and PPO reaches Kev+RL's final score (a crossover); not supported if Kev+RL learns at least as fast everywhere.
hypotheses.evidence: Kev+RL learned more slowly than the best PPO in 2 of 2 horizons; PPO did cross Kev+RL's curve.

hypotheses.statement: A JEV-style model is good at one-shot decisions, weaker at multi-step planning.
hypotheses.rule: Supported if Kev's gap to optimal (zero-shot and in-context, averaged) grows by >= 5 points from the shortest to the longest horizon; not supported if it shrinks or stays within 2 points.
hypotheses.evidence: Kev's gap to optimal goes from -0.1 (H=1) to 33.2 points (H=4).

hypotheses.statement: Calibrated confidence lets it hand off safely: sure on decidable calls, unsure on judgement calls.
hypotheses.rule: Supported if, at a 5% error budget, the best Kev arm automates >= 10 points more of the decidable calls than of the judgement calls and its ECE is <= 0.10; not supported if it automates no more decidable calls.
hypotheses.evidence: Kev-4B + context automates 0% of decidable vs 1% of judgement calls at a 5% error budget (ECE 0.21).

hypotheses.statement: Context without fine-tuning recovers part of the fine-tuning gain for free.
hypotheses.rule: Supported if Kev+context gains over zero-shot >= 25% of what Kev+RL gains (and more than 0); not supported if context doesn't help at all.
hypotheses.evidence: Context adds +1.7 points over zero-shot; RL adds -3.7.

hypotheses.statement: A System One model bridges regime changes: it covers the transition while RL is retrained.
hypotheses.rule: Supported if, when a planner declares the change, the bridge (Kev until retrained RL beats it) cuts transition regret by >= 25% vs the better RL-only strategy, for both shifts, both retraining modes and every PPO variant; not supported if it saves < 5% anywhere.
hypotheses.evidence: When a planner declares the change, bridging with Kev cuts transition regret by -101–-3% vs the better RL-only strategy, across shifts, retraining modes and PPO variants.

features.name: The question
features.why: Lead with the verdict. Researchers skim, and hiring managers skim harder.

features.name: Hypothesis scorecard
features.need: Trust: was this decided before or after looking?
features.why: Rules written before the runs, shown next to each verdict, prevent post-hoc storytelling.

features.name: The desk
features.need: Is this my world, or a toy?
features.why: Step through one scenario and reveal the hidden truth; grounds every later chart in a concrete decision.

features.name: Learning curves
features.why: Log x is the honest scale: RL needs orders of magnitude more experience, and a linear axis would hide Kev's starting point.

features.name: Sample-efficiency strip
features.need: How much experience before this is useful?
features.why: In planning, experience is the scarce thing. Decisions-to-threshold is the number a buyer budgets with.

features.name: Horizon dial
features.why: One small multiple per arm; the slope is the finding.

features.name: Hand-off view
features.need: What could I safely hand off?
features.why: Turns calibration, an abstract metric, into the planner's actual decision.

features.name: Decision replays
features.need: Show me a case where they differ.
features.why: One concrete disagreement is worth more than a chart.

features.name: Cost & latency
features.why: Accuracy without cost is half a decision.

features.name: Decisions log
features.why: Every design choice with its reasoning and the alternative rejected.

features.name: Transition timeline
features.need: Something changed this week: who decides until the model catches up, and what does the gap cost?
features.why: The question is about time, so the x axis is calendar weeks: a strip per strategy with the shift, the bridge's hand-back and the shaded regret, plus how fast each detector would have noticed.

features.name: Limitations
features.why: Synthetic world, one product, one model family, small horizons. Saying so is part of being credible.

decisions.decision: One environment with a horizon dial (1, 4, 12 weeks)
decisions.why: Makes 'one-shot vs multi-step' a controlled variable: only the horizon changes.
decisions.rejected: Separate one-shot and multi-step tasks, where task differences would confound the comparison.

decisions.why: Every note's reliability is known, so the Bayes-optimal planner, % of optimal and calibration are exact.
decisions.rejected: Real demand data with generated notes: realistic, but no ground truth to score against.

decisions.decision: Notes written by Phi-4-mini, a different model family from Kev's Qwen base
decisions.why: The text style can't favour the model under test. Train and test use different wording.
decisions.rejected: Templates only (too regular to test reading) or Qwen-written notes (a home-field advantage).

decisions.decision: Kev-4B as the open JEV stand-in
decisions.why: Apache-2.0, a JEV-compatible API, calibrated by default, and small enough to RL-train in budget.
decisions.rejected: Nimble-9B (slower to train) and the closed JEV API (no fine-tuning, no weights).

decisions.decision: PPO directly on Kev's pointer-head logits
decisions.why: Kev scores options instead of generating text, so its option distribution is already a policy.
decisions.rejected: Supervised fine-tuning on Bayes labels: that's imitation, not the RL comparison asked for.

decisions.decision: Three PPO variants (numbers / embeddings / parsed signals)
decisions.why: Separates 'can it read?' from 'can it learn?', the two things a JEV-style model bundles.
decisions.rejected: A single PPO baseline, which would leave the reason for any gap unknown.

decisions.decision: Two score scales: % of optimal and inbox value captured
decisions.why: Practitioners expect random = 0 / optimal = 100; planners ask whether reading beat their numbers-only tool.
decisions.rejected: One scale: random-anchored scores look high for any sane policy and hide the planner's question.

decisions.decision: Decidable vs judgement labels from the oracle
decisions.why: A decision is decidable when knowing the truth wouldn't change the call: a dominant strategy exists.
decisions.rejected: Labelling by the model's own confidence, which would make H4 circular.

decisions.decision: Regime changes measured as a bridge, not a contest (H6)
decisions.why: The realistic choice after a change isn't Kev or RL forever: it's who decides while retraining catches up.
decisions.rejected: Comparing stale RL with Kev only, which ignores that companies do retrain.

decisions.decision: One retraining curve, two calendar mappings (rebuilt simulator vs live experience)
decisions.why: Same warm-started PPO; the modes differ only in how fast new-world experience arrives, so training noise can't masquerade as a difference between them.

decisions.decision: An announced shift and a silent one
decisions.why: Text-readable changes are where a reading model should shine; silent ones test whether it notices from numbers, against a statistical detector calibrated to the same false-alarm rate.
decisions.rejected: Only announced shifts, which would flatter the model.

decisions.decision: A static report, no live inference
decisions.why: Cheap on the shared CPU-only lab box, instant to load and reproducible.
decisions.rejected: A live playground: it needs a GPU for little added insight; revisit after the results.

limitations: A synthetic world with one product and three demand regimes; real planning has many SKUs, lead times and constraints.
One decision-model family (Kev on Qwen3.5) at one size; the closed JEV may behave differently.
Horizons up to 12 weeks. Longer plans could widen or close the multi-step gap.
Regime changes are two stylised shifts at a plan boundary; real changes arrive gradually and mixed.
Live retraining pools 50 identical products; real portfolios are heterogeneous.
RL budgets are bounded (~100 Colab compute units): one Kev+RL seed, at two horizons, and its curves may not have converged.
Notes are generated text. They vary in wording but not in the messiness of real inboxes.
